# The Museum of Almost

The Museum of Almost stood at the end of a street so narrow that delivery drivers refused to enter it and pedestrians instinctively walked single file, even when they were alone. Above its door hung a wooden sign painted dark blue. The lettering had faded, but not enough to excuse the people who came in asking whether this was the lost-property office. Beneath the name, in smaller letters, were the opening hours: **Ten until four. Donations considered after midnight.** There was no admission fee. Visitors were asked only to wipe their feet and refrain from offering one another advice.

Mara Venn had worked there for eleven years. She sat behind a desk made from a door, cataloguing objects in a ledge-bound book and answering the telephone, which rang rarely and usually involved someone checking whether an almost could be donated anonymously. It could, though Mara preferred stories. An object without a story tended to sulk in its cabinet. A brass key became only a brass key; a train ticket became rubbish. With a story, both acquired weight.

The museum contained a violin that had never been played, though its owner had carried it to three auditions; an umbrella bought for an outdoor wedding at which it had not rained; a German dictionary whose first twelve pages were soft from use and whose remaining six hundred were crisp; and a teaspoon from a café in Vienna, where a man had almost proposed to his lover and had instead complained about the cake. There were letters, shoes, recipes, keys, maps, baby names written on envelopes, and one magnificent green hat. None of the objects was valuable in the ordinary way. All had cost someone a great deal.

Donors were invited to sit in the chair opposite Mara and explain what had nearly happened. Some spoke for hours. Others managed a sentence. Mara wrote everything first in pencil, because people often corrected themselves, and then in ink on a small cream card. She did not write that anyone had been foolish, cowardly, lucky, or wise. She had learned that an almost could contain all four without visibly changing shape.

Nothing supernatural occurred when an object was placed in its cabinet. The lights did not flicker. The donor did not rise from the chair magically restored. Usually the person simply sat for a while, looking at his or her empty hands. Sometimes there was relief. Sometimes there was a fresh and highly inconvenient grief. Mara offered tea, tissues, and directions to the night bus. She considered this last service as important as the others.

Her own contribution occupied the first cabinet, near the door. It was a railway ticket, one way, dated thirty-one years earlier. The destination was Durren, where there had been, and perhaps still was, an art school with a courtyard, four studios, and a policy of admitting a small number of students who could not afford the fees. Beneath the ticket, Mara’s card read: **Almost the eight-ten train. A seat by the window.**

She had been twenty-one. Her portfolio had contained twenty-two drawings, most of them of rooms: the kitchen after breakfast, the waiting room at the dentist’s surgery, her mother’s bedroom with the curtains drawn against the afternoon heat. Mara had liked drawing rooms just after people left them. A chair pushed back, a cup marked with lipstick, a book splayed open to keep its place—these seemed to her more truthful than faces. The school had offered her a place. Then her mother became ill, and the illness, which everyone initially described as temporary, developed habits and preferences. It liked mornings. It disliked stairs. It required forms to be filled in and medicines to be collected and someone to notice when an ordinary pain became a different kind of pain.

Mara had meant to defer for a year. The school could not hold her place. She had meant to apply again. Her younger sister, Celia, left home two years later with a rucksack, a camera, and an ability to make departure look like a form of generosity: Look how much room I am giving you. Celia sent postcards from ports and mountain towns, then from cities where she had learned to make large, difficult sculptures out of wire and cloth. Mara stayed. She worked in an insurance office, cared for her mother, and became skilled at interpreting the silences of doctors.

Her mother died four years ago, after an illness so long that grief had begun quietly unpacking its bags before the event itself. Mara had expected to feel either released or destroyed. Instead she felt administrative. There were telephone calls, forms, clothes to sort, a refrigerator containing too much soup. When the museum advertised for a night assistant, she applied because the hours seemed suitable for someone who had forgotten what to do with a day.

At one-seventeen on a wet October morning, Celia walked in.

Mara recognized her first by the way she closed the door: carefully, with one hand flat against it, as if preventing an animal from escaping. Then Celia lowered her umbrella and looked toward the desk. Her hair was shorter than in the photographs Mara had seen, and rain had darkened her coat. She had their mother’s eyebrows. This seemed, for a moment, an unnecessary thing to have brought back.

“You look tired,” Celia said.

“You look wet.”

“I am wet. I may also be tired. I haven’t decided whether to make an evening of it.”

Mara stood, though she did not come around the desk. They had last seen each other at the funeral, where they had been affectionate in public and precise with each other in private. Since then there had been messages on birthdays, an occasional conversation about legal matters, and once a postcard with no message except Celia’s initials and a drawing of a chair.

Celia set a small object on the desk. It was a brass key with a green cord threaded through it.

“I’d like to donate an almost,” she said.

“Of course you would.”

“That sounded judgmental.”

“It sounded like one in the morning.”

Mara brought out the tea things. While the kettle warmed, Celia walked slowly along the cabinets. She paused at the green hat and smiled. She did not look into the first cabinet, though she must have seen it.

The key, she explained when they were sitting down, was for a cottage outside Coimbra. She had gone there eleven years earlier with a woman named Ines. The cottage had two rooms, a unreliable roof, and a lemon tree growing so close to the kitchen window that Ines had been able to reach through and pick fruit without leaving the table. They had talked about renting it for a year. Celia had the key copied before either of them signed anything, because the copying machine was next to a bakery and she had liked the smell of the street.

“Then I got invited to Seoul,” she said. “For six months. Then there was Rotterdam. Ines said she wasn’t asking me never to go. She was asking me to stop treating every decision to go as if it had made itself.”

“Did you?”

“No. I became very interested in the word *necessary*. You can do a lot of damage with a word like that.”

Celia turned the key over. “I almost stayed.”

Mara took out a cream card.

“What happened?” she asked.

“I just told you.”

“After.”

Celia looked at her. “Fourteen cities, if you count generously. Three languages badly, one well. Work I’m proud of. Work I’d like to put in a river. Ines married someone who owns too many bicycles. I have a very good coat and no reliable sense of where I left it.”

Mara smiled despite herself.

“I came here,” Celia continued, “because I’m installing an exhibition at the old baths. Three months. There’s a flat with the exhibition, if you can call it a flat. It has a table, no chairs, and curtains the color of an unwell peach.” She hesitated. “I thought you might come and see it.”

The invitation was so small that Mara nearly missed it. She had imagined, without knowing she was imagining, that Celia would ask for something enormous: forgiveness, an explanation, the return of some earlier version of themselves.

“Thursday,” Mara said. “I could come on Thursday.”

Celia nodded, as if Thursday had been under negotiation for years.

Then she saw the ticket.

She did not ask permission before opening the cabinet. This irritated Mara, though not enough to stop her. Celia read the card and stood very still.

“You kept it,” she said.

“That is generally what a museum does.”

“You kept the ticket, but you threw away the drawings.”

“They weren’t good.”

“They were made by a twenty-one-year-old. They weren’t supposed to be finished.”

Mara felt an old heat rise in her. “You don’t get to come back and tell me which parts of my life I was allowed to keep.”

Celia closed the cabinet. “No. You’re right.”

The quick agreement disarmed Mara more than an argument would have. Rain ticked against the windows. Somewhere in the building a pipe knocked twice and was silent.

“I made it easy for you,” Mara said. “Being the one who left.”

Celia’s expression changed. “You made it easy for me to be the selfish one.”

“You managed that without assistance.”

“Yes.” Celia took a breath. “That was an old sentence. I brought it with me. I should have left it outside.”

Mara looked down at the blank card for the key. She thought of the Sundays when Celia telephoned and their mother held the receiver with both hands, laughing at descriptions of places Mara could not picture. She thought of the money Celia sent, always slightly more than necessary, and how efficiently Mara had resented it. She thought of Celia at twenty-three, calling from a station to ask whether their mother had mentioned her, and of Mara saying, “She’s asleep,” because she had been asleep, but not only because of that.

“I didn’t stay just for Mother,” Mara said.

“I know.”

“I was afraid.”

Celia’s mouth tightened, but not unkindly. “So was I.”

“You didn’t look afraid.”

“I was moving too quickly.”

This time they both laughed. It was not much of a laugh, but it altered the room.

Celia picked up one of Mara’s cataloguing cards. In the corner, without thinking, Mara had drawn the teaspoon from Vienna: three lines for the handle, an oval for the bowl, a small dark patch where the light struck it.

“You still do this,” Celia said.

“It helps identify the object.”

“It’s a drawing.”

“It’s a diagram.”

“A diagram with feelings.”

Mara took the card back. “If I start drawing again now, it will be bad.”

“Certainly.”

“That isn’t encouraging.”

“It’s extremely encouraging. You can skip the part where you wait to become someone who won’t be bad at it.” Celia leaned back. “I have been bad at things in several countries. It’s efficient. You can ask me anything.”

Near three o’clock, Celia prepared to leave. She did not ask whether Mara would come on Thursday, and Mara did not repeat that she would. At the door, Celia looked at the brass key on the desk.

“Keep that for a week,” Mara said. “On loan to the museum. You can have it back if you want it.”

“That isn’t your policy.”

“I’m considering a change in management.”

Celia smiled and went out into the rain.

She wrote about the museum: the green hat, the man with the teaspoon, the woman who had donated a pair of dancing shoes and returned six months later to report, without asking for them back, that she had enrolled in a class.

She wrote that she had been lonely. She wrote that she had been needed. She wrote that these facts had often occurred together and had not cancelled each other out.

Mara gave him a pencil.

Celia showed her the exhibition plans and complained about the lighting. Mara said almost nothing for twenty minutes, then made three suggestions. Celia accepted two of them and called the third sentimental. It was, Mara thought, a very successful visit.

Some choices narrowed a life. Some losses stayed losses. But beside the lives that had not happened, she made room for evidence of the ones that had: inconsistent, unphotogenic, often absurd, and rarely visible from the angle at which regret preferred to look.

Her own ticket stayed in the first cabinet. Beneath it were now seven cards. The last contained no writing, only a drawing of two cups on the museum desk, one chipped and one whole, with rain beyond the window and the door left slightly open.

Celia examined it one morning near closing time.

“The perspective is wrong,” she said.

“Yes.”

“The chipped cup looks as though it’s floating.”

“It was a difficult cup.”

Celia considered the drawing again. “Can I have the next one?”
